title: Security in Python: PyJWT, FastAPI dependencies, hashing and injection defences
seriesDescription: Prometheus and tracing, JWT and FastAPI auth, pytest and mocks. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: PyJWT encoding and verification, FastAPI OAuth2 bearer dependencies and role checks, CORS, password hashing with argon2, secrets, parameterised queries and command injection.
source: PyJWT documentation (decode, encode, algorithms, leeway); FastAPI documentation (Security, OAuth2, dependencies, CORS); argon2-cffi documentation; Python documentation (secrets, hmac, subprocess, sqlite3); SQLAlchemy documentation (text and bound parameters); OWASP cheat sheets

questions.prompt: Using PyJWT, verify `token` with the variable `public_key`: allow only `RS256`, require the audience `"orders-api"` and the issuer `"https://auth.example.com"`, and assign the claims to `claims`.
questions.model:
claims = jwt.decode(
    token, public_key,
    algorithms=["RS256"],
    audience="orders-api",
    issuer="https://auth.example.com",
)
questions.explanation: `jwt.decode` validates `exp` and `nbf` by default. Passing `algorithms` is mandatory in PyJWT 2.x precisely to block `alg=none` and algorithm-confusion attacks. Verified against PyJWT 2.14 with a generated RSA key.

questions.prompt: Using PyJWT, create an `RS256` access token for subject `user_id` that expires 15 minutes from now (use a timezone-aware UTC time), signed with `private_key`, and assign it to `token`.
questions.starter:
import jwt
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
questions.model:
token = jwt.encode(
    {"sub": user_id, "exp": datetime.now(timezone.utc) + timedelta(minutes=15)},
    private_key,
    algorithm="RS256",
)
questions.explanation: PyJWT converts datetime values for `exp`, `iat` and `nbf` into seconds since the epoch. Add iss and aud claims, and a `kid` header (`headers={"kid": ...}`) when you rotate keys.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI dependency `get_current_user(token)` that takes the token from `oauth2_scheme`, decodes it with `jwt.decode` (key `public_key`, `RS256` only), raises `HTTPException` 401 with the header `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` when `jwt.InvalidTokenError` occurs, and otherwise returns `claims["sub"]`.
questions.explanation: `OAuth2PasswordBearer` only extracts the token and returns 401 when the header is missing; the decoding is your job (verified with FastAPI `TestClient`). `ExpiredSignatureError` is a subclass of `InvalidTokenError`, so one except clause covers expiry too.

questions.prompt: True or false: in FastAPI, `OAuth2PasswordBearer` validates the JWT signature and expiry for you.

options.why: The class only reads the Authorization header.
Correct: it extracts the token string; verification happens in your dependency.

questions.explanation: Typical shape: token = `Depends(oauth2_scheme)`, then `jwt.decode` inside `get_current_user`, raising 401 on failure.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI dependency factory `require_role(role)` that depends on `get_current_user`, raises `HTTPException` 403 when `role` is not in `user.roles`, and otherwise returns the user.
questions.explanation: Use it as `@router.delete("/x", dependencies=[Depends(require_role("admin"))])`. A closure-returning dependency is the idiom; a class with `__call__` is an alternative.

questions.prompt: Match each FastAPI security helper with what it does.

right.text: Reads the bearer token from the Authorization header and documents the token URL
Reads a bearer credential without implying a login form
Like Depends but also declares the OAuth2 scopes the route needs
Adds cross-origin response headers for browsers

questions.explanation: None of the helpers verifies a JWT; verification is code you write (or a library you call) inside the dependency.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Calling `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` is safe for authenticating incoming requests.
questions.reason: With that option PyJWT returns the claims without checking the signature at all.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: an attacker could forge any claims. R is true and is exactly the danger.

questions.explanation: Use that option only for inspection, such as reading the `kid` header or claims in logs, never for access decisions.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: PyJWT rejects an expired token by default when decoding with a key and `algorithms`.
questions.reason: You must pass `options={"verify_exp": True}` to enable the expiry check.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true. R is false: the exp check is on by default and ExpiredSignatureError is raised.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Allow small clock drift with `leeway=10` (seconds) instead of disabling the check. A token 8 seconds past `exp` decodes with `leeway=10` and fails without it (verified).

questions.prompt: A service verifies with `jwt.decode(..., leeway=10)`. A token expired 8 seconds ago. How many more seconds, counting from now, will this call still accept it?
questions.explanation: The token is accepted until `exp` + leeway = 10 seconds after expiry. 8 seconds have passed, so 10 - 8 = 2 seconds remain.

questions.prompt: Using `argon2-cffi`, create a `PasswordHasher` named `ph`, hash the string `password` into `hashed`, and verify it with `ph.verify`.
questions.model:
ph = PasswordHasher()
hashed = ph.hash(password)
ph.verify(hashed, password)
questions.explanation: verify raises `VerifyMismatchError` on a wrong password instead of returning False, so catch it. The hash string embeds the algorithm, parameters and salt (it starts with `$argon2id$`), and `ph.check_needs_rehash(hashed)` tells you when to upgrade it after login.

questions.prompt: Write the Python statement that creates an unguessable URL-safe refresh token from 32 random bytes using the `secrets` module and stores it in `refresh`.
questions.explanation: Never use the random module for tokens: it is not cryptographically secure. Store only a hash of the token server-side.

questions.prompt: `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` encodes 32 random bytes with URL-safe base64 and no padding. How many characters long is the returned string?
questions.explanation: 32 bytes = 256 bits; base64 uses 6 bits per character, and ceil(256 / 6) = 43. Checked by calling the function. Hex encoding of the same bytes would be 64 characters.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Webhook signatures and API tokens should be compared with `hmac.compare_digest` rather than `==`.
questions.reason: The `==` operator on strings can return as soon as it finds the first differing character, so response time can leak how much of a guess was right.

whys.a: Correct: compare_digest takes constant time for equal-length inputs, closing the timing side channel.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Compute the expected value with `hmac.new(secret, body, "sha256").hexdigest()` and compare it to the header with `compare_digest`.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Rotating refresh tokens limits a stolen token to a single use.
questions.reason: The `secrets` module draws its random values from the operating system's secure random source.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the random source does not explain why rotation limits a stolen token; one-time use does.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Pair rotation with reuse detection: presenting an already used token revokes the whole family.

questions.prompt: Using the DB-API with `sqlite3` (cursor `cur`), run the query `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = <email>` safely with the variable `email` and assign `cur.fetchone()` to `row`.
questions.model:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,))
row = cur.fetchone()
questions.explanation: The one-element tuple needs the trailing comma. psycopg and mysql drivers use %s, sqlite3 uses ?. Never use f-strings to build SQL.

questions.prompt: Using SQLAlchemy, execute `text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email")` on the `session` with the variable `email` bound as a parameter, and assign the first row to `row`.

checks.label: binds email as a parameter dict

questions.model: row = session.execute(text("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :email"), {"email": email}).first()
questions.explanation: The :name placeholders are bound by the driver, so the value is data, not SQL. Interpolating email with an f-string into text() would reintroduce injection. The ORM query API binds values automatically.

questions.prompt: A service must run the external tool `convert` on a filename that comes from an upload. Which call is safest?

options.text: `subprocess.run(f"convert {filename} out.png", shell=True)`, after checking the file extension.
options.why: A shell parses metacharacters such as ; and $() hidden in the name.

options.text: `os.system("convert " + filename + " out.png")` because it is the shortest form available.
`subprocess.run("convert " + filename, shell=True)` inside a try block that logs the exception.
options.why: Logging errors does not stop the injection from running.

options.text: `subprocess.run(["convert", filename, "out.png"], check=True)` with the default shell setting.
options.why: Correct: an argument list is not parsed by a shell.

questions.explanation: Also validate or generate the filename yourself, and run external tools with least privilege and a timeout.

questions.text: jwt.decode(token, key, {1}=["RS256"], {2}="orders-api", {3}="https://auth.example.com") rejects tokens signed with another algorithm, issued for another audience, or issued by another party.
questions.explanation: Each of the three checks closes a different attack: algorithm confusion, token replay across services and tokens from an untrusted issuer.

questions.prompt: Add Starlette's `CORSMiddleware` to the FastAPI app `app` so that only `https://app.example.com` may call it from a browser, with `GET` and `POST` methods and credentials allowed.
questions.explanation: With credentials, browsers reject a wildcard origin, so list origins explicitly. CORS is enforced by the browser only; keep server-side authentication on every route.
